title: Claude Code & agentic work
note: Durable agentic-engineering practice: the loop and its verifier, context, extensions, the trust boundary, scaling out, and what the evidence shows. Tool details change monthly; settings, syntax and the tool landscape live in the official docs. Refresh quarterly.

concepts.s: A coding agent runs a loop of gather context, plan, act and verify; its output is capped by the verifier you give it, it amplifies whatever discipline you already have, and its permissions define the blast radius.

x.b:
• Loop: context in, plan, edit and run tools, verify, repeat. Anthropic's Claude Code docs describe gather context, take action, verify results.
  • Verifier: the agent stops when work looks done; a runnable check decides what "done" means.
  • Amplifier: DORA 2025 found AI magnifies existing strengths and dysfunctions.
  • Trust boundary: anything the agent reads can steer it, so permissions and isolation set the worst case.
Trap: Optimizing prompts while the verifier is weak. Better prompts can't fix an agent that can't tell when it's wrong.
An agent keeps shipping broken dashboards: add a check that diffs rendered output against an expected screenshot before tuning the prompt.

cards.q: An agent's output quality plateaus despite better prompts. Which part of the map do you strengthen?
cards.a: The verifier: give it a runnable check (tests, reconciliation, screenshot diff) that defines done.

cards.q: What does DORA 2025's amplifier finding imply for a team with weak testing?
cards.a: AI will magnify the weakness: more throughput with more instability; fix the practices first.

concepts.s: Separate read-only exploration and planning from implementation so the agent doesn't solve the wrong problem, and end each unit of work in a reviewable commit.

x.b:
1. Explore in plan mode: read and answer questions, change nothing.
  2. Plan: files, flow, risks; edit the plan before approving.
  3. Implement against the plan with tests.
  4. Commit with a descriptive message and PR.

Every task prompt carries goal, context, constraints and done criteria. Anthropic's rule: if you can describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.

For larger features, have the agent interview you and write SPEC.md, then implement in a fresh session; a precise spec pays off more than watching the build. Match model and effort to difficulty.
Trap: Correcting the same mistake repeatedly in one session. After two failed corrections, clear and restart with a better first prompt; failed attempts pollute context.
"Fix the refill-rate metric" becomes: goal (match finance's definition), context (metric file, last month's numbers), constraints (no schema change), done (test reproduces finance's figure).

cards.q: When does Anthropic suggest skipping plan mode?
cards.a: When you could describe the whole diff in one sentence.

cards.q: The agent failed the same fix twice. What next?
cards.a: Clear the session and restart with a better first prompt that includes what you learned.

concepts.s: The highest-leverage practice is a check the agent can run itself (tests, build, linter, reconciliation, screenshot), because without one you become the verification loop.

x.b:
• Escalating gates: ask it to run the check; a goal condition re-checked each turn; a Stop hook that blocks finishing until the check passes; a fresh-context subagent that tries to refute the result.
  • Ask for evidence (command, output, screenshot), not a claim of success.
  • Claude Code's creator Boris Cherny called a verification loop his top tip, claiming 2-3x better results (X posts, Jan 2026).

Trap: Agents suppress failing signals. Say "fix the root cause, don't silence the error".
Trap: Flaky or slow checks: an agent can't reason about a test that passes at random.
For a pipeline: row counts and checksums reconciled against a known-good source, schema tests, and a rendered dashboard compared with an expected image.

cards.q: An agent reports "all tests pass" but the feature fails end to end. What gate was missing?
cards.a: An end-to-end check run as a user would (browser or reconciliation), with evidence required.

cards.q: How can you stop an agent from ending its turn before a check passes?
cards.a: A Stop hook that runs the check and blocks completion until it passes.

concepts.s: Have the agent write a failing test first, then the minimum code to pass it, and protect the tests, because a precise executable target makes cheating visible.

x.b:
Simon Willison calls it red/green: watch the test fail, then pass. Kent Beck's rules (2025): one failing test at a time, minimum code to pass, then refactor; never mix structural and behavioral changes in one commit.

Beck's warning signs: loops, functionality he didn't ask for, and cheating such as disabling or deleting tests.

Trap: Tests written after the code that mirror it pass by construction.
Trap: A diff touching tests and code together: a weakened assertion looks like a fix. Review test changes separately, or block test edits with a hook during implementation.
Bug: wrong refill count. Prompt: write a failing test with last month's case, confirm it fails, then fix without editing the test.

cards.q: An agent's fix passes after it edited an assertion. Which warning sign is this?
cards.a: Cheating: changing the test instead of the code; review test changes separately.

cards.q: Why write the failing test before the fix?
cards.a: It gives the agent a precise target and shows the fix actually changed behavior.

concepts.s: Everything the agent knows sits in one finite context window, so keep bulky reads out, reset between tasks, and compact deliberately.

x.b:
• Startup loads system prompt, CLAUDE.md, memory, skill descriptions and tool names; reads and output accumulate.
  • Anthropic frames context as an attention budget with diminishing returns (context rot).
  • Tools: /context to inspect, /clear between unrelated tasks, /compact with a focus to summarize, subagents to keep large searches and logs out.

Trap: Important rules given only in chat can be lost at compaction; put them in CLAUDE.md.
Trap: Pasting a giant log that refills the window after every summary.
Investigating a failing job: a subagent reads 40 MB of logs and returns a ten-line diagnosis; the main session stays clean.

cards.q: You're about to read thousands of log lines to find one error. How do you protect the main context?
cards.a: Delegate the read to a subagent that returns only the conclusion.

cards.q: A rule you stated early in a long session stopped being followed. Why, and the fix?
cards.a: It was likely lost at compaction; put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md.

concepts.s: Checkpoints let you rewind the agent's file edits and conversation, but they don't undo shell commands or anything outside your machine, so commits stay your real safety net.

x.b:
• Claude Code checkpoints each prompt's file edits made through its edit tools; /rewind (or Esc twice) restores code, conversation or both, or summarizes part of the session.
  • Not restored: files changed by shell commands (rm, mv, cp), usually subagent edits, and edits made outside the session.
  • Never restorable: databases, APIs, deploys and other remote side effects.
  • /branch copies the conversation so you can try an alternative and keep the original.
Trap: Trusting rewind after the agent ran a migration or deleted files with rm. Gate remote and destructive actions with permission rules instead.
The agent ran a bad schema migration on the dev database. Rewind restores the code, not the database; you need the migration's down script.

cards.q: The agent deleted files with rm. Will /rewind bring them back?
cards.a: No: shell-command changes aren't checkpointed; recover from git.

cards.q: What protects remote side effects that rewind can't undo?
cards.a: Permission rules or hooks that gate those actions before they run.

concepts.s: Put what the agent should always know in short instruction files, and anything that must never happen in deterministic hooks or permission rules.

x.b:
• CLAUDE.md (or your tool's equivalent, such as AGENTS.md): build commands, conventions, gotchas; Anthropic suggests under about 200 lines per file.
  • Path-scoped rules load only when matching files are touched; skills hold occasional procedures.
  • Instructions are context, not enforcement. Hooks run every time; PreToolUse hooks can block a tool call.

Trap: Writing a guardrail as prose ("never push to main"). Use a deny rule or hook.
Trap: A 600-line CLAUDE.md: adherence drops as it grows.
CLAUDE.md says how to run tests; a PreToolUse hook blocks edits to migrations/; a rule file scoped to api/** holds API conventions.

cards.q: Where does "never edit files in migrations/" belong?
cards.a: In a permission deny rule or PreToolUse hook, since CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement.

cards.q: Your CLAUDE.md is 600 lines and adherence is poor. What do you do?
cards.a: Cut it toward ~200 lines; move area-specific guidance to path-scoped rules and procedures into skills.

concepts.s: Turn every repeated agent mistake into durable infrastructure (a rule, a skill or command, a script, a hook or a CI check) and prune it when models improve.

x.b:
Mitchell Hashimoto calls this harness engineering: each time an agent errs, add an AGENTS.md line or a tool so it never recurs. A useful ladder as a rule proves important: prompt, instruction file, skill or command, then hook, linter or CI check. Each step trades flexibility for reliability.

Shared in the repo, these files become team infrastructure: one engineer's lesson becomes every agent's default.

Trap: Rule pile-up: an agent ignoring a rule usually means the file is too long. Prune.
Trap: Never revisiting rules after a model upgrade: each one encodes an assumption about what the model can't do (Anthropic, March 2026).
The agent forgets the test command twice: add it to CLAUDE.md. It keeps formatting wrong: add a PostToolUse hook. It touched prod config: add a deny rule.

cards.q: The same mistake recurred three times despite a CLAUDE.md line. What control makes it impossible?
cards.a: A deterministic control: a hook, linter or CI check.

cards.q: Why prune instructions after a model upgrade?
cards.a: Workarounds for old weaknesses cost context and can now mislead.

concepts.s: Review is the bottleneck, so keep agent changes small, review them in a fresh context, and merge only code a human can explain and owns.

x.b:
• Writer/reviewer: a second session with fresh context reviews, because a model is biased toward code it just wrote (Anthropic best practices).
  • Tell AI reviewers to flag only gaps affecting correctness or requirements; they otherwise always find something.
  • Andrej Karpathy's observed failure modes (Jan 2026): unchecked assumptions, no pushback, bloated abstractions, dead code.

Trap: Rubber-stamping a large green PR. Size work so a human can actually review it.
Trap: Treating every AI review finding as mandatory: it inflates code with defensive branches.
Patient-facing or PHI code: line-by-line human review stays mandatory. Low-risk internal tooling with strong tests is where reading less is defensible.

cards.q: Why use a fresh-context session to review agent code?
cards.a: The writing session is biased toward its own code; a fresh context reviews more skeptically.

cards.q: An AI reviewer flags twelve issues on a sound PR. How should you instruct it?
cards.a: Flag only gaps that affect correctness or stated requirements.

concepts.s: Use CLAUDE.md for what to know, skills for how-to loaded on demand, MCP for tools into outside systems, subagents for isolated work, and hooks for what must always happen.

x.b:
• CLAUDE.md / rules: always-on knowledge.
  • Skills (SKILL.md): name and description stay in context; the body loads when relevant. Mark side-effecting skills user-invoked only.
  • MCP servers: tools and data from external systems; a good CLI is often more context-efficient.
  • Subagents: own context, tools and model; return a summary.
  • Hooks: deterministic handlers at lifecycle events.
  • Plugins bundle these to share.

A subagent (except a fork) sees only CLAUDE.md and your delegation prompt, not your conversation, so the prompt must carry the task context.

Trap: Vague skill descriptions: the agent loads the wrong skill or none.
Trap: Installing skills or MCP servers from untrusted sources; they can carry malicious instructions or code.
A database: MCP server for queries, a skill describing the schema and query patterns, a hook that formats SQL after each edit.

cards.q: You want SQL formatted after every edit, no exceptions. Which extension?
cards.a: A hook (PostToolUse on edits): it runs every time, unlike instructions.

cards.q: A deploy procedure the agent should run only when you ask. Which extension and setting?
cards.a: A skill with model invocation disabled, so only you can trigger it.

concepts.s: Most agent productivity comes from fewer approval prompts, and the safe way to get it is isolation plus least privilege, not clicking yes faster.

x.b:
• Anthropic reported users accept 93% of permission prompts, so manual approval decays into click-through (March 2026).
  • Spectrum: manual approval, allowlisted safe commands, classifier-based auto mode, full isolation in containers or cloud sandboxes with restricted network.
  • Anthropic's auto mode: 0.4% false positives, but it missed 17% of a small set of real overeager actions; not a substitute for review on high-stakes infrastructure. As of Nov 2026, interactive terminal and VS Code sessions start in auto mode on every plan unless a mode is set; headless defaults vary, so set the mode explicitly.

Order: PreToolUse hooks run first and can block in any mode; then deny, ask, allow rules, with deny and ask holding even when bypassing permissions. A hook's allow can't override a deny.
Trap: Skipping all permissions on a laptop with cloud credentials in the environment.
Healthcare: no PHI or production credentials in the agent's environment, read-only scoped database roles, synthetic data, egress limited to approved hosts.

cards.q: Why does adding more approval prompts not make agents safer?
cards.a: People accept nearly all of them (93% per Anthropic), so approval becomes click-through; isolation works better.

cards.q: When is skipping approvals reasonable?
cards.a: Inside an isolated sandbox with restricted network and no sensitive credentials.

concepts.s: Anything an agent reads can act as an instruction, so never combine private data, untrusted content and an outbound channel in one agent.

x.b:
Simon Willison's lethal trifecta: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. With all three, an attacker can exfiltrate data. Detection is unreliable; remove a leg instead, usually by cutting network egress or isolating the data.

Clinejection (early 2026): an AI issue-triage workflow fed issue titles into a prompt with shell access; a crafted title led, via Actions cache poisoning, to stolen publishing tokens and a tampered npm release on about 4,000 machines (Cloud Security Alliance).
Trap: Wiring an agent with write or shell access to public issue or PR text.
A triage bot on public issues gets only label and comment permissions, runs on collaborator-only triggers, and holds no publishing secrets.

cards.q: Name the three legs of the lethal trifecta.
cards.a: Private data access, exposure to untrusted content, and an external communication channel.

cards.q: Your agent reads web pages and has your cloud keys. Cheapest fix?
cards.a: Remove a leg: take the credentials out of its environment or block outbound network.

concepts.s: Parallel agents multiply throughput only when tasks are independent, each agent has its own checkout, and you start no more than you can review.

x.b:
• Isolation: one git worktree, clone or cloud session per agent.
  • Good parallel work: research spikes, explanations of existing code, small chores, well-specified tasks, scouting a hard task you won't merge.
  • Boris Cherny reports running about 5 local and 5-10 web sessions and abandoning 10-20% (Jan 2026).

Trap: More sessions than you can review: output piles up and quality drops. Set a WIP limit.
Trap: Shared mutable resources (one dev database, port, cache) collide outside Git.
A fan-out over 300 files: pilot the prompt on 3 files, fix it, then run the batch with scoped tools.

cards.q: Two agents edit the same repo and keep clobbering each other. Fix?
cards.a: Give each its own worktree or clone (and separate shared resources).

cards.q: What sets the right number of parallel agent sessions?
cards.a: Your review capacity: a WIP limit equal to what you can review well.

concepts.s: Multi-session agent work succeeds when state lives on disk (spec, feature list, progress log, git), each session starts fresh and reorients from files, and a separate evaluator checks the work.

x.b:
• Anthropic's long-running harness (2025): an initializer writes a feature list (all failing), a progress log and a startup script; each later session reads them, does one feature, commits and updates the log.
  • Anthropic (March 2026): agents grading their own work praise it even when it's mediocre; a separate evaluator tuned to be skeptical is far easier to get right.
  • Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph loop pipes the same prompt into a fresh agent session repeatedly, with the plan, specs and tests on disk as memory and backpressure.

Trap: Weak tests: the loop happily ships code that compiles and does the wrong thing.
Trap: Unbounded spend: cap iterations or budget, and commit every iteration so you can reset.
A migration of 200 independent dashboards: a feature list with 200 items, one per session, each checked by a screenshot comparison before it is marked passing.
Can a brand-new session learn the project state from files in under a minute?

cards.q: A multi-day agent project declares itself done with half the features. What prevents this?
cards.a: An explicit feature list with one feature per session and a separate evaluator marking items passing.

cards.q: What does the Ralph loop rely on instead of a long context?
cards.a: State on disk (plan, specs, tests, git) and a fresh session every iteration.

concepts.s: Run agents non-interactively in scripts and CI for repeatable jobs, with tightly scoped tools and permissions because no human approves each step.

x.b:
• Headless mode (claude -p) takes a prompt and returns output; loop it over files or tasks.
  • CI integrations let agents review PRs, triage issues or fix failing checks on events or schedules.
  • The Agent SDK builds custom agents on the same harness.
  • Non-interactive runs load the repo's hooks and project MCP servers without a trust prompt; run with minimal configuration and explicit allowlists.
Trap: A CI agent with broad tools, triggered by any user, sharing caches with release workflows: the Clinejection pattern.
A nightly job runs a headless agent to update dependency pins, runs tests, and opens a PR; merge goes through the normal protected path.

cards.q: What is the key risk difference between interactive and headless agent runs?
cards.a: No human approves each step, so tools, permissions and inputs must be scoped in advance.

cards.q: A nightly agent job should never push to main. How do you enforce it?
cards.a: Give it a narrow identity that can only open PRs, with rulesets protecting main.

concepts.s: Controlled evidence on coding-agent productivity is thin and mixed: self-reports and throughput rise, but the best trial found a slowdown experts didn't perceive, and stability tends to fall.

x.b:
• METR 2025 RCT: experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with early-2025 tools while believing they were faster. Its February 2026 follow-up leaned toward a speedup, but selection bias (developers wouldn't work without AI) made it unreliable.
  • DORA 2025 (about 5,000 respondents): about 90% use AI; adoption relates to higher throughput and lower delivery stability.
  • Anthropic internal study (Dec 2025): merged PRs per engineer per day up 67% (measured); self-reported gains rose to about 50% (survey: non-anonymous, recall bias).

Trap: Quoting the 19% slowdown as current truth: it measured early-2025 tools.
Trap: Treating self-reported speedups as evidence; METR showed perception and measurement diverge.
A vendor deck claims 55% faster coding from a survey. Ask: controlled? Which outcome? Did change failure rate move?

cards.q: What was METR's key finding beyond the 19% slowdown?
cards.a: Developers believed AI had sped them up even though it slowed them down.

cards.q: Throughput rose after AI adoption. What does DORA 2025 suggest checking?
cards.a: Delivery stability (change failure rate, rework), which tended to worsen.

concepts.s: Judge agent productivity by outcome metrics that include rework, not by self-report or PR counts.

x.b:
• Track lead time to production, change failure rate, time to restore, review latency, and the share of agent PRs reverted or heavily rewritten.
  • Compare like-for-like work; agents shift the mix toward small fixes and work that would not otherwise exist.
  • Time a few matched tasks with and without the agent.
Trap: PR counts reward volume; a flood of small PRs can hide falling quality.
Monthly: agent-authored PRs, % reverted within 14 days, median review time, incidents traced to agent changes.
What would convince you the agent made things worse?

cards.q: PRs per engineer doubled after adopting agents. What else must you check before calling it a win?
cards.a: Rework and stability: reverts, change failure rate, review latency, incidents.

cards.q: Why are self-reported speedups unreliable?
cards.a: METR's trial showed developers felt faster while measured time increased.

concepts.s: Public benchmarks show agents improving on clean, well-specified tasks; only a trial on your own repositories, checks and review standards tells you what a tool will do for you.

x.b:
• METR's time horizon is the length of task (in skilled-human time) a model completes with 50% reliability on well-specified tasks. It has doubled every several months, but it means coin-flip success on clean briefs, not a reliable day of work.
  • SWE-bench-style leaderboards cluster at the top, risk contamination, and move with scaffolding as much as the model.

Run your own: 10-20 recently closed tickets of mixed types, the same instructions and checks for each tool, scored on checks passed, review minutes to mergeable, rework, cost and policy violations. Repeat after major model releases.
Trap: Choosing a tool from demos or a few leaderboard points.
For a BI team: a dbt model change with tests, a slow-query fix checked by its plan, and a dashboard change verified by screenshot.

cards.q: What does a 50% time horizon of 14 hours mean?
cards.a: Coin-flip success on well-specified tasks that take a skilled human about 14 hours, not reliable completion of a real day's work.

cards.q: Two tools differ by 2 points on a coding leaderboard. How much weight?
cards.a: Little: scaffolding and contamination move scores that much; test on your own tickets.

concepts.n: Skill formation and the changing role
concepts.s: Heavy delegation can erode the skills you need to supervise agents, so use interaction patterns that keep understanding in the loop as the role shifts toward specification, design and review.

x.b:
Anthropic's January 2026 randomized trial: 52 mostly junior engineers learning a new library scored 50% on a follow-up quiz with AI assistance versus 67% coding by hand, with the biggest gap in debugging, and weren't significantly faster. Learning survived when they asked conceptual questions or requested code with explanations; full delegation and AI-first debugging hurt.

Karpathy reports review and writing skills diverge; Willison defines agentic engineering as experts amplified by agents, distinct from vibe coding.
Trap: Using the agent as first-resort debugger while learning a new stack: the lowest-scoring pattern.
On work you want to learn from, write the spec and tests yourself, use generate-then-explain, and debug the first new class of bug by hand.

cards.q: Which AI usage pattern scored lowest in Anthropic's trial?
cards.a: Iterative AI debugging; full delegation and progressive reliance also scored low.

cards.q: A junior relies on agents for everything. Which practice protects their skill?
cards.a: Require them to explain every agent-written change and to write specs and tests themselves.
